meta.titre: Economic Rent: transfer earnings, quasi-rent and taxation
meta.sous_theme: Economic rent, transfer earnings and quasi-rent

sections.contenu_markdown: A famous footballer in Cameroon may earn many times more than he would earn in any other job, while a plot of land in a busy part of Douala earns its owner a great deal simply because it cannot be moved or made larger. Economists call the surplus in such cases economic rent, and it has nothing to do with paying rent on a house. Examiners test the definition, the link with the elasticity of supply, the difference between rent and quasi-rent, and the question of whether such surpluses should be taxed. This course covers each of these.

items: Elasticity of supply measures how much the quantity supplied responds to a change in price.
The factors of production are land, labour, capital and enterprise, and each earns a reward: rent, wages, interest and profit.
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up.
A perfectly inelastic supply curve is vertical: the quantity does not change when price changes.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### Definitions
- **Economic rent** is the payment to a factor of production **above its transfer earnings**. It is a surplus.
- **Transfer earnings** are the **minimum payment needed to keep the factor in its present use**, equal to what it could earn in its **next best alternative use** (its opportunity cost). If the payment fell below this amount the factor would move to another use.

$$\text{total earnings} = \text{transfer earnings} + \text{economic rent}$$

$$\text{economic rent} = \text{actual earnings} - \text{transfer earnings}$$

Economic rent is different from the **contractual rent** paid by a tenant for a house or a shop in everyday language.

### Elasticity of supply decides the size of rent
| Supply of the factor | Transfer earnings | Economic rent |
|---|---|---|
| Perfectly inelastic (vertical) | Zero | The whole of earnings (pure economic rent) |
| Inelastic | Small share | Large share |
| Elastic | Large share | Small share |
| Perfectly elastic (horizontal) | The whole of earnings | Zero |

The more specialised and scarce a factor is, the less elastic its supply is and the greater the share of its earnings that is rent.

### Land with one use
If land has only one use, its supply is perfectly inelastic: it cannot go elsewhere, so its transfer earnings are zero and **all its income is economic rent**. The payment is then determined by demand: if demand rises, the rent per hectare rises, but the quantity of land does not change.

### Representing rent with a supply and demand curve
With price on the vertical axis and the quantity of the factor on the horizontal axis, economic rent is the area **between the price line and the supply curve**, up to the equilibrium quantity. Transfer earnings are the area under the supply curve.

### Any factor can earn rent
Rent is not confined to land. A highly skilled worker, a unique machine or a talented entrepreneur may earn much more than the next best use of their services, and the surplus is economic rent.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Questions on temporary surpluses and short-run scarcity
variantes.contenu_markdown: **Quasi-rent** (Marshall's term) is a surplus earned in the **short run** by a factor whose supply is fixed in the short run, for example machines or a skilled trade when demand rises quickly. The surplus comes from a shortage of supply. In the long run the supply can be increased: more machines are built or more workers are trained, the surplus is competed away and earnings fall back to the level that is just enough to keep the factor in its use, which is transfer earnings. Quasi-rent is therefore temporary, whereas the rent on a fixed plot can persist.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Questions on land of different quality
variantes.contenu_markdown: Ricardo explained that land of different fertility earns different rents. When the price of the product covers the cost on the poorest (marginal) land only, the marginal land earns no rent, and better land earns a rent equal to the extra revenue its higher yield brings. For the economy as a whole, the rent on land with only one use is price-determined, not price-determining. For a single industry that must attract land from other uses, the rent it pays is a cost of production.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Evaluation questions on whether such surpluses should be taxed
variantes.contenu_markdown: A tax on pure economic rent does not reduce the quantity supplied, since the factor has no alternative use, so it raises revenue without distorting supply, and many see it as fair when the surplus comes from scarcity rather than effort. The difficulty is that transfer earnings are hard to measure, a tax that falls on transfer earnings can push the factor into another use, and a very high tax may weaken the incentive to improve the land or to acquire skills.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A firm hires five skilled workers, and each is paid the same wage of 180,000 FCFA a month. The lowest wage that would keep each worker in this job, because of the next best job each has, is 100,000, 120,000, 140,000, 160,000 and 180,000 FCFA a month.

(a) Calculate the transfer earnings and the economic rent of each worker and in total.
(b) Calculate the share of economic rent in total earnings.
(c) Explain how the share would change if the supply of these workers were more elastic.

etapes.justification: Transfer earnings are the minimum acceptable pay; rent is the extra.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Rent of a worker = wage paid - transfer earnings.

etapes.justification: The wage is the same for all five, so rent differs by worker.
Transfer earnings and rent must add up to total earnings.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Total earnings = 5 x 180 = 900. Transfer earnings = 100 + 120 + 140 + 160 + 180 = 700. Economic rent = 900 - 700 = **200 thousand FCFA a month**, as 80 + 60 + 40 + 20 + 0.

etapes.justification: The share compares the rent with the total payment.
Differences in transfer earnings between workers mean that supply is upward sloping, which is why some rent exists.
etapes.resultat_markdown: If the workers were more alike and could move easily to equally good jobs, their transfer earnings would be close to 180 and the rent share would fall; if they were all unique with no alternative, the whole 900 would be rent.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) The rents are 80, 60, 40, 20 and 0, so the total economic rent is 200 thousand FCFA a month, with transfer earnings of 700. (b) Rent is 22.2 per cent of total earnings. (c) More elastic supply means transfer earnings closer to the wage paid, so the rent falls as a share of earnings; with perfectly elastic supply the rent would be zero.

items.erreur_markdown: Using 'economic rent' to mean the rent paid on a house or shop.
items.pourquoi_faux: Contractual rent is a payment for the use of a building. Economic rent is a surplus above transfer earnings.
items.correction_markdown: Define economic rent as earnings above what is needed to keep the factor in its present use.

items.pourquoi_faux: Any factor whose supply is not perfectly elastic can earn economic rent, including labour with a rare skill.
items.correction_markdown: Give an example from labour, such as a top musician or player.

items.erreur_markdown: "All of the income of every piece of land is economic rent."
items.pourquoi_faux: This holds only for land with a single use. Land that can be used in other ways has transfer earnings, so only the surplus is rent.
items.correction_markdown: Say that the whole income is rent when supply is perfectly inelastic, and only the part above the next best use otherwise.

items.erreur_markdown: Mixing up transfer earnings and economic rent.
items.pourquoi_faux: Transfer earnings are the opportunity cost that keeps the factor in its use; rent is what is left above it. They add up to total earnings.
items.correction_markdown: Write: economic rent = actual earnings - transfer earnings.

items.pourquoi_faux: It arises because supply is fixed in the short run. In the long run supply adjusts and the surplus disappears.
items.correction_markdown: State that quasi-rent is temporary and is competed away in the long run.

items.enonce_markdown:
A popular singer earns 5,000,000 FCFA a month. In the best alternative job she could earn 1,200,000 FCFA a month.

(a) Calculate her transfer earnings and economic rent.
(b) Calculate the percentage of her earnings that is economic rent.

Three farms grow cassava with the same cost of 600,000 FCFA per hectare, not counting any rent. The price of cassava is 50,000 FCFA a tonne. The yields are 20 tonnes per hectare on Farm 1, 16 on Farm 2 and 12 on Farm 3.

(a) Calculate the revenue of each farm and the rent that each can pay.
(b) Explain why Farm 3 pays no rent.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Revenue: Farm 1 = 20 x 50,000 = 1,000,000; Farm 2 = 16 x 50,000 = 800,000; Farm 3 = 12 x 50,000 = 600,000 FCFA. Rent = revenue - cost: **400,000, 200,000 and 0 FCFA**.

(b) Farm 3 is the marginal land: its revenue just covers its costs, so it earns no surplus. Better land earns a differential rent that comes from its higher fertility; if the price of cassava rose, Farm 3 would earn rent too and poorer land would come into use.

items.enonce_markdown:
A plot earns its owner 600,000 FCFA a year as farmland. Its best alternative use is market gardening, which would earn 450,000 FCFA a year. The government is considering (i) a tax of 30% on the whole 600,000 FCFA income and (ii) a tax of 30% on the economic rent only.

(a) Calculate the transfer earnings and economic rent of the plot.
(b) Calculate the owner's net income under each tax and say what the owner will do.
(c) Discuss whether taxing economic rent is a good idea.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Transfer earnings = **450,000 FCFA**; economic rent = 600,000 - 450,000 = **150,000 FCFA**.

(b) (i) Tax = 0.30 x 600,000 = 180,000, so net income = 420,000, which is **below** 450,000: the owner switches to market gardening and supply of farmland falls. (ii) Tax = 0.30 x 150,000 = 45,000, so net income = 555,000, which is **above** 450,000: the owner stays and supply is unchanged.

(c) Award marks for: a tax on pure rent does not change supply (efficiency) and takes a surplus not earned by effort (equity); problems: transfer earnings are hard to measure, a tax on the whole income distorts the use of the land, and very high taxes can weaken the incentive to improve the land; judgement: **a tax on genuine economic rent is efficient in theory, but it is hard to apply accurately**.

items_markdown: Economic rent = actual earnings - transfer earnings; transfer earnings are the minimum payment that keeps a factor in its present use (its next best alternative).
The less elastic the supply of a factor, the greater the share of its earnings that is rent; with perfectly inelastic supply (land with one use) all earnings are rent.
Any factor can earn economic rent, not only land; it is different from the contractual rent paid for a building.
Quasi-rent is a temporary short-run surplus of a factor whose supply is fixed in the short run; it disappears in the long run as supply adjusts.
A tax on pure economic rent does not reduce supply, but it is hard to measure transfer earnings.
